summary: Profiles Internet mail for voice messaging, so that different voice mail systems can exchange messages using ordinary email. This second version of the Voice Profile for Internet Mail replaces RFC 1911. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 3801.

eli5.summary: Voice mail boxes from different companies could not normally swap messages. This lets them send voice recordings to each other as if they were email attachments.

questions: how can voice mail be sent over email
how do voice mail systems exchange messages
can voice mail work with email
subtitle: Standard format for sending voice mail messages over Internet email.

tldr.problem: Voice mail systems from different vendors traditionally could not exchange messages with each other. There was no standard way to send voice recordings between phone systems using the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: VPIM defines a profile of Internet mail (MIME and ESMTP) that lets voice mail systems package voice recordings and fax documents as email messages. It specifies message formats, addressing for numeric mailboxes, content types for audio and fax, and transport using ESMTP.
tldr.outcome: Voice mail systems can now interoperate over the Internet, allowing voice messages and faxes to be sent between different vendors' systems. The RFC was quickly updated as RFC 3801 with security and other improvements.

today: RFC 2421 was superseded by RFC 3801 in June 2004, which added important security clarifications, support for additional encodings, and other improvements. The core concept of VPIM—using Internet mail protocols for voice messaging—remains valid, though modern voice over IP systems have largely replaced traditional voice mail.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
VPIM (Voice Profile for Internet Mail) is a profile of Internet mail protocols that lets voice mail systems exchange messages over TCP/IP networks. This second version replaces RFC 1911 with improvements based on implementation experience.

Voice mail systems are special-purpose computers that answer calls, record messages, and notify users. Traditionally, they used analog networking based on telephone signals (DTMF). This RFC defines how voice mail systems can instead use the standard Internet mail protocols (MIME for message format and ESMTP for transport) to exchange voice and fax messages.

VPIM is not an IETF working group product, but rather from the EMA VPIM Work Group, which includes representatives from major voice mail vendors. The profile is designed to work within corporate intranets and even across the public Internet, though with some limitations.
sections.eli5: Voice mail machines usually talk to their own company's other machines. This document explains how to make machines from different companies talk to each other using email as the medium.

sections.title: Design Goals and System Limitations
sections.content:
VPIM is designed with realistic constraints of voice mail systems in mind:

  • Limited text support: Voice mail systems are designed to deliver audio, not text. Text messages cannot be easily displayed and require text-to-speech or text-to-fax conversion.
  • Simple architecture: Voice mail machines act as combined message transport agents, message stores, and user agents. They typically do not relay messages or preserve the full semantics of Internet messages.
  • Limited addressing: Voice mail systems traditionally use 16 or fewer numeric characters for mailbox IDs because numbers are entered from a telephone keypad. Alphanumeric addresses may not be supported.
  • Machine-parsable errors: Error messages must be machine-readable so the system can speak helpful responses to users whose only access is a telephone.
  • No distribution lists: Voice mail systems implement local alias lists with reply-to-sender and error-to-sender behavior, not Internet-style distribution lists.

Despite these limitations, the profile aims to be robust enough for use across the global Internet while remaining simple enough for rapid deployment.
sections.eli5: Voice mail systems are designed to handle voice, not text. They think in phone numbers, not email addresses. They are simple machines without fancy features. VPIM had to work with these real-world limitations.

sections.title: Message Format and Content Types
sections.content:
VPIM messages use the multipart/voice-message MIME content type as their top level. This container bundles voice, fax, and metadata together. Within a VPIM message, several content types are permitted:

  • Audio/32KADPCM: The standard voice encoding. This is a 32 kilobit-per-second ADPCM audio format. All implementations must support sending and receiving this format. It can be used for the main voice message, a spoken name (about 10 seconds), or a spoken subject (about 20 seconds).
  • Image/TIFF: For sending facsimile documents. Only TIFF-F (TIFF for Facsimile) profile is allowed, with one image strip per page.
  • Text/Directory (vCard): An electronic business card containing the sender's name, telephone number, email address, and optionally a recording of their spoken name. The vCard MUST use version 3.0 and MUST include TEL and EMAIL attributes.
  • Message/RFC822: For forwarding complete messages or replying with the original content.

Messages MAY include a spoken delivery notification, and content may be sent as multipart/mixed when additional non-voice components are needed.
sections.eli5: A VPIM message is like a box with compartments: one for the voice recording, one for a fax, one for a business card, one for attached forwarded messages. The voice recording format is always the same so all machines understand it.

sections.title: Message Addressing and Delivery
sections.content:
VPIM addresses are based on RFC 822 email addresses but adapted for voice mail:

  • Numeric mailbox: The local part (before the @) can be numeric (e.g., 2722@lucent.com).
  • International telephone numbers: A mailbox starting with a plus sign (+) is an international phone number in E.164 format (maximum 15 digits), optionally with an extension (e.g., +16137637582@vm.nortel.ca).
  • Special addresses: The address postmaster@domain MUST exist for system diagnostics. The address non-mail-user@domain indicates an unreachable sender (like a telephone answering machine) to which replies should not be sent.

Message headers include From (originator), To and Cc (recipients), Date (with timezone), and optional fields like Importance, Sensitivity, and Disposition-Notification-To (for receipt confirmation). The Sensitivity header, if present, indicates privacy: a Private message MUST NOT be forwarded and SHOULD NOT include the original content in replies.
sections.eli5: Voice mail systems use phone numbers as mailbox names. A message can say 'do not forward this' or 'send me a receipt when you listen to this' just like email can.

sections.title: Transport and Interoperability
sections.content:
VPIM messages are transported using ESMTP (Extended SMTP), the same protocol used for ordinary email. Voice mail systems MUST implement these ESMTP commands:

  • EHLO: Announce capabilities.
  • MAIL FROM: Specify the originator's address (used for delivery status notifications).
  • RCPT TO: Specify each recipient.
  • DATA: Transfer the message body.
  • QUIT, RSET: Connection management.

Systems SHOULD support BDAT (binary data) for efficient binary transport and PIPELINING to send multiple commands before waiting for responses. The SIZE extension allows the server to declare its maximum message size, important since voice messages can be many megabytes.

VPIM is designed to be robust against gateways that do not understand MIME. A compliant system MUST accept multipart/voice-message but can fall back to treating it as multipart/mixed if needed. Detailed conformance requirements specify that systems must handle delivery status notifications and message disposition notifications (MDN) for receipt confirmation.
sections.eli5: Voice mail messages travel over the same email network as regular emails. The sending system tells the receiving system upfront how big the message is so it can decide whether to accept it.
